blurb.explorer: The white board with lots of little holes.
blurb.builder: A board full of holes that grip wires. Holes in the same little row are already joined together underneath.
blurb.engineer: Solderless prototyping board. Columns A-E and F-J of each row are connected internally; the centre channel separates them. The long side rails are the power buses.

blurb.explorer: Bendy wires that carry the zap.
blurb.builder: Wires that carry electricity from one hole to another.
blurb.engineer: Insulated 22AWG links. Colour is convention only: red for positive, black for ground.

blurb.explorer: Wires with little teeth that bite.
blurb.builder: Clip-on wires. These are how you connect the breadboard to a lemon.
blurb.engineer: Croc-clip test leads. The bridge between breadboard holes and anything that isn't a component - fruit, nails, foil.

blurb.explorer: The thing that pushes the zap around.
blurb.builder: The pump that pushes electricity around the loop. Red wire is the push side, black is the return.
blurb.engineer: 9V DC source. Internal resistance is low enough that a direct short gets hot quickly - always include a limiting resistor.

blurb.explorer: Four fat batteries in a box.
blurb.builder: Gives a gentler push than a 9V battery, so it's kinder to LEDs.
blurb.engineer: 6V pack. Lower voltage means a smaller limiting resistor and more margin before an LED cooks.

blurb.builder: A light that only works one way round. The long leg goes to the push side.
blurb.engineer: Light-emitting diode. Vf about 2.0V, 20mA max. Long leg is the anode (+), short leg and the flat spot are the cathode (-). Needs a series resistor.

blurb.builder: Like the red light, but green - and it needs a slightly bigger push.
blurb.engineer: Vf about 2.1V, 20mA max. Same polarity rules as the red LED.

blurb.explorer: Press it to make things happen!
blurb.builder: A gate for electricity. Pressed = open, let go = shut.
blurb.engineer: Momentary SPST tactile switch. The four legs are two pairs; the pairs are always connected, and pressing joins the pairs. Straddle the centre channel.

blurb.explorer: A tiny helper with three legs.
blurb.builder: A magic tap. A tiny trickle into the middle leg lets a big flow through the other two.
blurb.engineer: NPN BJT. A small base current controls a much larger collector current - hFE is roughly 100. Flat face towards you: legs are usually E, B, C. Check your part number.

blurb.explorer: Makes a red dot. Only with a grown-up!
blurb.builder: A very bright, very thin beam of light. Adults only, and it always points at the wall.
blurb.engineer: 650nm diode laser module, typically 3-5V with a built-in driver resistor. If yours is a bare diode, it MUST have current limiting or it dies instantly.

blurb.builder: Slows the electricity down so the light doesn't burn out.
blurb.engineer: 220 ohms. Colour bands: red-red-brown. Pairs with a 6V supply and a red LED for about 18mA.

blurb.builder: The everyday brake for LEDs. Use this one if you're not sure.
blurb.engineer: 330 ohms. Colour bands: orange-orange-brown. With a 9V supply and a red LED this gives about 21mA - close enough.

blurb.builder: A stronger brake. Makes the light dimmer but safer.
blurb.engineer: 1000 ohms. Colour bands: brown-black-red. Also the standard base resistor for switching a transistor.

blurb.builder: Such a strong brake that almost nothing gets through. We use it for the fruit experiments.
blurb.engineer: 1,000,000 ohms. Colour bands: brown-black-green. Used as the pull-down on the transistor base so the touch switch doesn't float on.

blurb.explorer: A silver nail for the lemon.
blurb.builder: The silver electrode. Zinc is the metal that gives its bits away.
blurb.engineer: Zinc-coated steel. In the fruit cell the zinc oxidises - this is the negative electrode.

blurb.explorer: An orange-brown wire for the lemon.
blurb.builder: The copper electrode. Use real bare copper wire, not a penny - modern pennies are only copper-coloured on the outside.
blurb.engineer: Bare copper strip or heavy wire, positive electrode of the fruit cell. Post-1982 US pennies are zinc-cored, so they make a poor copper electrode.

blurb.builder: Measures how hard the electricity is pushing (volts) and how hard something fights back (ohms).
blurb.engineer: DMM. Use DC volts for the fruit cell, and resistance mode with a fixed 2cm probe gap for the conductivity leaderboard.

blurb.builder: Sour fruit. The juice is full of acid, which is what lets electricity move through it.
blurb.engineer: Citric acid electrolyte. The most reliable fruit cell - roughly 0.9V open-circuit with zinc and copper.

blurb.builder: Works like the lemon but not as strongly. Cooking it first makes it work better!
blurb.engineer: Phosphoric acid electrolyte, higher internal resistance than a lemon. Boiling breaks down cell walls and measurably improves output.
